record.original_question: Conjecture: Suppose that for a fixed positive integer k at least half of the elements of a finite group G have order k. Then G is solvable.

evidence.quote: Conjecture: Suppose that for a fixed positive integer k at least half of the elements of a finite group G have order k. Then G is solvable.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finite group and let $k$ be a fixed positive integer. For each integer $n \geq 1$, let $\Omega_n(G) = \{g \in G : |g| = n\}$ denote the set of elements of $G$ of order exactly $n$. Suppose that
$$|\Omega_k(G)| \geq \tfrac{1}{2}|G|,$$
that is, at least half of the elements of $G$ have order equal to $k$. Prove or disprove: under this hypothesis, $G$ must be solvable.
artifact.status_search_result: A recent paper "Finite groups with many elements of the same order" disproves the conjecture in its original form by exhibiting non-solvable finite groups in which at least half of the elements have a common order k for various composite values of k (e.g., k = 9, and various composites divisible by 2 or 3). The conjecture is shown to hold for k = 1, 2, 3, 4, and for prime powers p^a with p > 3, but fails in general.

status_evidence.title: Finite groups with many elements of the same order
status_evidence.snippet: the original conjecture fails by presenting some counterexamples ... for all k > 1, it is always possible to find a finite non-soluble group where at least 2/15 of the elements have order k
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is disproved in general; counterexamples exist for many composite k, while it remains true for k=1,2,3,4 and for prime powers p^a with p>3.

status_evidence.title: The Kourovka Notebook (problem list)
status_evidence.snippet: Kourovka Notebook collection of unsolved problems in group theory
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture appears as a problem in the Kourovka Notebook problem collection.
